For a complete extraction workflow, use a PDK notebook from [Choose a simulation](../examples.qmd#getting-started).
This backend reference uses the `snapshot` from [source observations](source-observations.qmd).
The branch asks for Electrostatic terminal response rather than resonant modes.
The public OrPen [Xmon notebook group](../examples.qmd#public-inputs) owns the
component example; this lesson explains the reusable SCGSim stages.

A Terminal identifies a conductor Net whose excitation enters the native
matrix. Physical Ground identifies other conductor Nets. Grounding the outer
solution boundary is a separate physical choice, not another spelling of a
conductor ground. Here the Xmon pad is the terminal and its already assigned
`Ground` Net is the physical ground:

```python
from pathlib import Path
from scgsim.palace import ElectrostaticSim

sim = ElectrostaticSim()
sim.set_plan(snapshot)
sim.set_output_dir(Path(".artifacts/public-xmon-electrostatic"))
sim.add_terminal("xmon", net_id="xmon_pad")
sim.add_ground(net_id="Ground")
sim.set_electrostatic(
    save_fields=0,
    unassigned_conductor_policy="error",
    exterior_boundary_policy="none",
)
sim.set_mesh(quality_threshold=0.01)
```

`set_mesh(...)` chooses the sizing `recipe`, the `mesher` options (algorithms and
geometry order), the repair `budgets` and the `quality_threshold`. This example
keeps the default recipe and states the default threshold, so you can see where
to change it. Geometric order describes the mesh representation and is
independent of Palace's FEM order. The controls, their defaults and what happens
when the mesh cannot reach the threshold are in the shared
[Palace mesh controls](../specs/palace-electrostatic-sgb.qmd#palace-mesh-controls).

The terminal and ground selectors are exact final Net IDs. They are not
geometric center guesses. The explicit `error` policy makes uncovered conductor
components an input error; the alternative supported `ground` policy grounds
unassigned components. Choose the policy for your experiment. The exterior is
left ungrounded here; `exterior_boundary_policy="ground"` is a separate model
and requires the explicit error policy. [The contract](../specs/palace-electrostatic-sgb.qmd)
owns these choices and their index-map meaning.

## Declare when refinement has converged

Adaptive refinement is off by default (`amr_max_passes=0`). To refine, give a
pass limit, then state which numbers must stop changing and by how much. The
thresholds below show the form; choose your own from what the circuit question
needs:

```python
from scgsim.palace import Capacitance, ErrorIndicator

sim.set_numerical(order=2, amr_max_passes=6)
sim.set_convergence(
    Capacitance.element("xmon", "xmon").within(relative=1e-3),
    ErrorIndicator().below(1e-2),
    minimum_converged_passes=2,
)
```

Each pass is one Palace solve; pass 1 solves the mesh `mesh()` writes. The
first criterion holds at a pass when `C[xmon][xmon]` changed by at most 0.1 %
since the pass before, so it can first hold at pass 2. The second holds when
Palace's error indicator is at most 0.01. The run has converged at the first pass
where both have held for two passes in a row; with six refinements there are
seven solves, enough for that.

`write_config()` checks the declaration against the config before it writes
anything: `Capacitance.element("xmon", "pad")` is refused because the simulation
has no terminal `pad`, and `set_numerical(amr_max_passes=1)` is refused because
two solves cannot give two passes in a row of a change. A stated
`amr_tolerance` is refused too: with a declaration the criteria decide, and the
refusal names the `ErrorIndicator().below(...)` line to write instead.

In this version Palace still runs all seven solves. When you read the returned
run, `result.convergence.verdict` and the trust report say at which pass the
run had converged, for example:

> Converged at pass 4 of the 7 passes run: every criterion held at passes 3 to
> 4, 2 in a row. Last to hold: C[xmon][xmon], from pass 3. 3 more passes ran
> after it, up to amr_max_passes.

The [convergence declaration](../specs/palace-electrostatic-sgb.qmd#convergence-declaration)
lists every quantity (the diagonal, sub-diagonals, the whole matrix, Surface EPR
by interface kind) and every check.

## Select the geometry approximation and build inputs

The bound snapshot already supplies the outer envelope. Route B is the default
finite-metal preparation, and Surface EPR is computed only when you request it,
so this setup meshes as it stands:

```python
mesh_path = sim.mesh()
config_path = sim.write_config()
print(mesh_path, config_path)
```

For a Route-A study, call `sim.set_route("A")` before meshing. Route A makes the
film conductors zero-thickness sheets, while finite bodies such as bumps keep their
volume. The approximation profile says what happens to the thickness a film had: without one, `set_route("A")` uses `thin_film`, which
removes the thickness and takes no parameters. For `substrate_face`, which
preserves physical face coordinates, or `metal_gap_equivalent`, the separate
supported two-face normalization, pass the profile with its explicit
`film_bindings`: `sim.set_route("A", approximation_profile=profile)`. Route B
needs no call. Consult the [geometry contract](../geometry-sgb.qmd) before
changing that approximation. Surface films are optional postprocessing specifications, with attributed
thickness/permittivity/loss assumptions rather than inferred material
measurements. Their inset margins are cut into the geometry, so request them
with `set_surface_epr(specs)` before `mesh()`; see the
[margin contract](../specs/palace-eigenmode.qmd#surface-epr-margins).

The mesh is a real preparation operation. It can fail natively, and it stops
with `MeshRepairError` when a tetrahedron stays below the quality threshold. Writing config
binds terminal and Ground attributes to that mesh. Inspect the exact index map
alongside the config: schema v3 distinguishes physical Ground from exterior
Ground, so you can tell which conductor and boundary policy was lowered.
After meshing, `sim.mesh_summary()` exposes detached native generation
observations, including mesh controls, element/region counts and exact mesh
identities. Those records describe the mesh; they do not decide whether its
discretization is adequate for a study.
Before meshing, `sim.input_summary()` shows the input `mesh()` builds from (the
plan with the simulation's vacuum region applied) with the terminals, grounds
and policies; the [source summary](source-observations.qmd) is the view of the
plan alone.

Next [inspect the prepared mesh](solver-observations.qmd) if useful, then
[prepare and execute the handoff](execute.qmd). On return,
[resolve it](returned-results.qmd) before reading the capacitance matrix. Native
terminal/excitation ordering and units remain authoritative; a prepared config
contains no measured capacitance. State which terminal response your circuit
question needs, then read that matrix entry and its available refinement
history in the [research interpretation sequence](returned-results.qmd#interpret-for-scq-use).
Retain terminal excitation, physical/exterior ground choices, actual criteria
and native status; a native stopping flag alone does not decide whether the
capacitance is adequate for that circuit-model use.
